A_target.statement:
Let $f, g: \closedint a b \to \R$ be [[Definition:Continuous Real Function|continuous]] and $c \in \closedint a b$.
Then $\displaystyle \int_a^b \map f x \rd x$ exists, and:
:$\displaystyle \int_a^b \paren {\lambda f + \mu g} = \lambda \int_a^b f + \mu \int_a^b g$
:$\displaystyle \int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$

B_source.statement:
Let $I$ be a [[Definition:Finite Set|finite]] index set partitioned as $I = I_1 \cup I_2$.
Then:
:$\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop \in I} \paren {\lambda x_i + \mu y_i} = \lambda \sum_{i \mathop \in I} x_i + \mu \sum_{i \mathop \in I} y_i$
:$\displaystyle \sum_{i \mathop \in I} x_i = \sum_{i \mathop \in I_1} x_i + \sum_{i \mathop \in I_2} x_i$

object_map.reformulation: View the integral as a limit of finite Riemann sums, so finite-sum properties pass to the limit.

validity_conditions: f continuous (hence Riemann integrable), so the limit of Riemann sums exists.
Linearity and additivity hold for each finite Riemann sum and are preserved under the limit.
This is generalization, not pure transport: the limit step is genuine new content, not a renaming.
proof_plan:
From [[Continuous Real Function is Riemann Integrable]]:
:$\displaystyle \int_a^b f = \lim_{\norm P \mathop \to 0} \sum_{i \mathop = 1}^n \map f {\xi_i} \paren {x_i - x_{i - 1} }$
the limit of [[Definition:Riemann Sum|Riemann sums]].

Each Riemann sum is a finite sum, hence linear in $f$.
For a subdivision containing $c$, the index set splits into the parts in $\closedint a c$ and $\closedint c b$.
By [[Combination Theorem for Limits of Functions|linearity of limits]], and taking subdivisions containing $c$, these properties pass through the limit.

Hence the integral is linear and additive over subintervals.
{{qed}}
